q: Fixed costs per unit vary with the quantum of traffic.
e: The correct answer is Inversely. Fixed costs per unit vary inversely with the quantum of traffic, so option B is correct. Total fixed cost stays the same for a given scale of capacity, so when traffic (NTKMs/PKMs) rises the same fixed cost spreads over more units and the per-unit figure falls. This inverse relationship is the reason better asset utilisation brings down unit cost. This provision exists for a practical reason in day-to-day railway working; keeping that practical picture in mind makes the fact far easier to retain than memorising it in isolation.

q: Operating Ratio Can be worked out as
e: The correct answer is (Working expense + depreciation and Interest)/Earnings. Operating Ratio = (Working expenses + depreciation + interest) / Earnings, so option B is correct. A lower operating ratio means better financial performance; the Board watches it as the headline efficiency indicator.

q: Which method is used to calculate Depreciation on Capital asset?
e: Depreciation on capital assets in Indian Railways is calculated by the Straight Line Method, so option A is correct. Under this method the asset's cost (less residual value) is spread evenly over its normal life, giving an equal annual charge. Under the fixed instalment (straight line) method, an equal amount of depreciation is charged every year over the asset's useful life, so the book value falls uniformly.

q: Apportionment of joint cost is required in Costing

options.B: Spread over of the production units
options.C: Same assets are being utilised for rendering a variety of services
options.D: Production process is not restricted to the factory premises

e: Option C (Same assets are being utilised for rendering a variety of services) is the correct choice. Apportionment of joint cost is required in costing because the same assets are utilised for rendering a variety of services, so option C is correct. One track, one locomotive fleet and one signalling system serve coaching, goods and EMU traffic together, so joint expenses cannot be traced to a single service and must be apportioned on a suitable basis. This shared-asset character is the heart of railway costing. Notice how precisely the correct option is worded.

q: The distinguishing feature of the terminal expenses is

options.A: These costs are not directly related to a particular function.
options.B: These expenses are not affected by the lead of traffic
options.C: These costs increases or decreases in direct proportion with the volume of traffic
options.D: These cost always relate to a particular scale of capacity

e: These expenses are not affected by the lead of traffic — that is the right answer. The distinguishing feature of terminal expenses is that they are not affected by the lead of traffic, so option B is correct. Terminal costs arise at the originating and terminating ends (booking, handling, documentation) and stay the same whether the consignment travels 100 km or 1,000 km. This distance-independence is what separates terminal cost from line haul cost. Notice how precisely the correct option is worded.

q: Line Haul cost consists of the following
e: Option C (Traction, Transportation, Track & Signalling cost) is the correct choice. Line haul cost consists of traction, transportation, and track and signalling costs, so option C is correct. These are the costs of actually hauling the train over the section — energy and locomotives (traction), train operation (transportation), and the permanent way with signalling. Packing and marshalling belong to terminal and marshalling costs, not line haul.
